new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened A's saved file (+.): header 'Kplang (Prang), Ghana [Refer to Ethnologue]', numerals 1-2000 exactly as A lists them (1 kɔ̃ / ɛkʊ́nkɔ́, 2 áɲɔ, 3 asa, 4 aná, 5 ɛnʊ́.. 10 ídú, 20 ɛ́dʊ́ɲɔ, 100 ɛ́lɛ́fa, 1000 ɛ́ɡ͡bʊ́ŋ), then 'Linguist providing data and dateː Dr. J. Andy Ring. May 15, 1995. GILLBT (The Ghana Institute of Linguistics, Literacy and Bible Translation), Ghana' and 'Other comments: Kplang has a decimal system of counting similar to that of Krache, Low tone unmarked.' A's quote is verbatim apart from the '..' elision and the bracketed sample it flags as '[data, e.g...]'. the Internet Archive itself was could not be reached by automated download today, but I independently download…
new_statements.relation_note: Tone-marked numeral list (acute = H, unmarked = L) with explicit convention note 'Low tone unmarked'; no stress marks, no statement on stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: First-hand GILLBT transcription of Kplang numerals marks High tone with an acute accent and leaves Low tone unmarked, i.e. the field linguist records a lexical H vs L tone contrast on Kplang words (e.g. asa 'three' all-Low vs aná 'four' L-H vs ídú 'ten' H-H). Nothing is said about stress/accent. This is a transcription-convention note on a 40-item numeral list, not a phonological description: number of tones beyond H/L, downstep, and any stress are not addressed.
new_statements.identity_note: Headed 'Kplang (Prang), Ghana [Refer to Ethnologue]'; data credited to J. Andy Ring of GILLBT, the same source Pozdniakov 2018:360 credits for Kplang; comment compares the system to Krache (a River Oti North Guang sister), consistent with kpla1238. Not the Yeji dialect of Chumburung. | Same dataset as A's work 1 (the Internet Archive 2011 copy), listed only because A reported the live host unreachable: the live page adds the speaker figure (c. 1,600) and location (Brong-Ahafo: Sene district south of Volta lake; Pru district, Yeji town) that tie it to Ethnologue's kph entry, and rephrases the tone note. Not an additional source; a stable live URL and corroborating copy for work 1.

sources.citation: Barker, Peter. 2011 (undated online draft; Word file created 2011-06-11, fieldwork 2008-2010). 'Eastern Pru District' and 'Sene Peninsula': sub-chapters Yeji, Prang (Kplang), Bassa, Dwan, Nkomi, Wiase [file '6 GUANG MASTER.doc']. In: Northern Ghana Peoples (www.northernghanapeoples.co.uk), the author's online revision of Barker 1986, Peoples, Languages and Religion in Northern Ghana (Accra: GEC/Asempa). 20 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on Kplang phonology. States only that Yeji and Prang (Kplang) are two small indigenous Guang peoples with 'their own related but separate languages', that Hausa is the trade language in Prang town and Twi the regional lingua franca. Useful solely as identity/location/population evidence and as confirmation that no literacy or Bible-translation (hence orthography) work exists for Kplang.

sources.citation: Painter, Colin. 1967. The distribution of Guang in Ghana, and a statistical pre-testing on twenty-five idiolects. Journal of West African Languages 4(1): 25-78.
sources.note: Nothing. Transcription conventions (p.28) mark only tone (h/m/l after each word); no stress statement. Crucially p.31: 'I hope later to add lists for Efutu.., Kwame Danso (Nchumuru), Prang and the Dahomey dialects. All but the latter I have heard and talked about but not yet recorded' -- i.e. Prang/Kplang is NOT among the 25 idiolects; Glottolog's only 'Kplang' reference contains no Kplang data.
